Phenomenology therefore differs from psychology as dynamics differs from statics.
Psychology studies the result of the development of a quality independently of the development that produced it—that is, it does not study the quality as a result.
Phenomenology studies a quality in its becoming, its development, and as the result of that becoming.
In short, Phenomenology differs from psychology because psychology is not historical.
As for history, we can say the reverse: it differs from Phenomenology because it is not psychological.

Since psychology abstracts from time and history, it cannot, without Phenomenology, know in principle that it is examining the “soul” of a particular historical age. It will therefore tend to assume that it is studying the eternal and unchanging qualities of humanity “in general.”
History, by contrast, consciously studies human beings belonging to a particular age and assumes that it is studying only those people.
When it speaks about the Greeks of the age of Pericles, for example, it deliberately puts aside the French of the revolutionary period, and vice versa.
In other words, history is not interested in what belongs to humanity “in general,” and therefore has little interest in human “psychology.”

Of course, the historian talks about what a historical individual—or even a crowd, a class, or an entire people—“wants,” “feels,” “thinks,” “says,” “experiences,” and is “conscious of.” The historian also describes their “self-consciousness.”
But in doing so, the historian studies only what the people in question think, want, say, and so forth—not what an “opinion,” an “action,” or the “capacity for speech” is as such.
Phenomenology, by contrast, reminds the historian that there is such a thing as historical inheritance.
A new historical age does not “fall from the sky.” It is conditioned by the age that preceded it, and therefore ultimately by all previous ages.
Once this has been recognized, Phenomenology can point out that what a person of a particular historical age thinks and does is, in a certain sense, also characteristic of humanity “in general.”
By examining the desires, thoughts, and so forth of a particular historical age, we can also discover what “desire as such,” “thought as such,” and so forth are.
Properly human qualities—the very qualities history studies—are certainly not unchanging. They are historical, which means that under different historical conditions they would be different.
But precisely because they are historical, they do not simply disappear. Once they have emerged, they remain present in humanity.

“Christian” consciousness may be different from “pagan” consciousness. But because Christian consciousness is historically the heir of pagan consciousness, it still contains what pagan consciousness produced—even if in modified form, even if as a negation, or even if only as a memory.
In this sense, the “psychic” qualities of the pagan also belong to humanity in general.
But this “humanity in general” is itself historical.

Its “psychology” therefore cannot be fully understood without studying its “history.” We cannot forget that human qualities did not all belong to humanity “from the beginning.” They emerge during the historical process and change along with it.
To understand them, we need to know when, how, and why they emerged and changed.
By studying history, we can understand this “psychology.”
But to do that, we have to study history very differently from the way the “scientific” historian does.

The scientific historian is quite properly not interested in this psychology. He therefore excludes whatever belongs to it, or at least does not consciously draw the conclusions that would give us knowledge of it.

History differs from Phenomenology, then, because it does not try to derive a “psychological” knowledge of humanity from knowledge of human history. Phenomenology, by contrast, treats history as the material from which such knowledge can be obtained.
Phenomenology is therefore, so to speak, a union or synthesis of history and psychology.
Phenomenological psychology differs from scientific psychology because it is historical. Phenomenological history differs from scientific history because it makes use of psychology.
So we could equally call Phenomenology phenomenological psychology or phenomenological history. We could also define it as a historical psychology or a psychological history of humanity.
But even these descriptions can cause serious misunderstanding.
Psychology and history are not separated from one another by accident.
The psychologist cannot simply add history to psychological research: there is, so to speak, no room for it within psychology as normally conceived.
Likewise, ordinary historical research has no need to add psychology in the sense intended here.

To produce this “synthesis” of psychology and history, we therefore have to change both of them fundamentally. We must treat the human “psyche” and history very differently from the way scientific psychologists and historians do.

If we define Phenomenology as “historical psychology” or “psychological history,” then, we must immediately add that it differs fundamentally from both history and psychology in their ordinary senses.
For that reason it is better not to use these expressions at all.
So what, exactly, distinguishes Phenomenology from psychology and history? And why does it differ from them?
Ultimately, it differs because it is precisely Phenomenology.
If it is in some sense a “history,” it is the history proper to Phenomenology—and therefore, in some sense, also a “psychology.”
And if it is in some sense a psychology, it is a psychology proper to Phenomenology—and therefore, in some sense, also a “history.”

To understand this, however, we must return again to the question: in what sense is Phenomenology actually Phenomenology—that is, a discourse or science of “phenomena,” which, as we already know, are in a certain sense both historical and psychological?

To understand more clearly the distinctive sui generis character of the object and theme of Phenomenology, it is useful to compare them with the object and theme of the systematic Philosophy for which Phenomenology prepares us and to which it serves as an introduction.
We have seen that Philosophy must, in principle, answer every question a human being can ask.

But among the enormous number of possible questions, we need to distinguish those that are specifically philosophical—in the broad sense, whether phenomenological or systematic—from those that a non-philosopher can in principle answer, whether an ordinary “naive” person or a scientist.
The distinctive feature of these non-philosophical questions is that, in the minds of the people asking them, they concern “reality itself”—what contemporary philosophers call “objective” reality.
If an ordinary person or a scientist is talking about a birch tree, for example, they talk precisely about the birch tree and nothing else. Everything else is, so to speak, forgotten.
The birch is separated from all the other objects in the world. At most, the world remains an undefined “background” that apparently need not be examined any further.

For the person talking about the birch, neither the “ideal” world of words, judgments, mathematical formulas, fictional characters, and so forth, nor the human, technical, social, and political world exists.
Indeed, even the person who is talking seems, in his own eyes, to have disappeared.

More generally, a non-philosophical answer responds only to what the question immediately asks about. It deals only with the object of the question and leaves aside everything “outside” that object, including, in particular, the question itself and the person asking it.
Of course, the object of a non-philosophical question can in principle be almost anything.
It might be an isolated thing in the real natural world. It might even be the natural world as a whole. But in that case the real human world and the “ideal” world are excluded.

The ideal world can also become the object of non-philosophical questions. But then the answer will contain nothing concerning the real world. A mathematician studying a mathematical object, for example, effectively forgets that mathematics is created by a real human being living in the natural world.
Finally, the theme of a non-philosophical investigation can even be a human being or the real human world.
But then, say, the natural world—or, as always, the person carrying out the investigation—is put to one side.
When an ordinary person writes an autobiography, or when a scientist conducts psychological “introspection,” the object of study is indeed himself.
Yet even leaving aside the fact that while reflecting on himself he partly forgets the surrounding world, he also leaves behind one part of himself: precisely the part that is doing the reflecting.
In other words, he observes himself, so to speak, “from the outside,” just as an ordinary person observes a pine tree or a scientist observes Julius Caesar or a parabola.
The ordinary person or botanist looking at a birch tree forgets himself entirely.

The scientific psychologist then observes this observer, who might even be the psychologist himself. But in doing so, the psychologist not only forgets the birch as something existing outside the observer. He also forgets himself, just as completely as the observer of the birch did.
His theme is only the study of the “object itself.”
For the observer of the birch, that object is the birch. The observation itself, and the observer himself, remain outside the field of observation.
In short, as we have already said several times, the ordinary person and the scientist deal with abstractions, not with concrete reality.
A human being can speak only about the reality of which he is speaking.
Concrete reality therefore includes not only the ideal or real, natural or human object of discourse, but also the discourse itself and the human being who produces it.
The ordinary person abstracts from these things and speaks only about the object. He therefore speaks about an abstraction.
He therefore calls this abstraction—the object of the ordinary person or scientist—a phenomenon or appearance.

Now, ordinary people and scientists can in principle speak about virtually anything. And because whatever they speak about is, for the philosopher, a phenomenon or appearance, it follows that literally anything can function as a “phenomenon.”
A phenomenon might be an isolated thing in the real natural world, or the natural world as a whole.
It might be an individual human being, a particular aspect of human life or activity, whether practical or theoretical, or the historical world as a whole.
It might be an isolated ideal entity or the entire “ideal world.”
Ordinary language does not use the word phenomenon quite so broadly.

We may speak, for example, of a volcanic eruption as a “natural phenomenon,” but we do not normally call a birch tree a phenomenon. We speak of Greek tragedy as a “literary phenomenon,” but not usually of Euclidean geometry as a “mathematical phenomenon,” and so on.
These boundaries in ordinary language are obviously contingent and have no fundamental importance. There is no serious objection to extending the word phenomenon more widely.
The real issue is that the everyday and philosophical meanings of the term do not fully coincide.
When an ordinary person or scientist speaks of a “natural phenomenon,” the emphasis falls on the word nature.
Nature itself is supposed to manifest itself in a volcanic eruption, and if we knew all natural phenomena, we would supposedly know what nature itself is.
When the philosopher uses the same expression, however, the emphasis falls on phenomenon.
For the philosopher, a volcanic eruption is not primarily a phenomenon of nature. It is an appearance of nature to human beings.
The philosopher therefore takes the word phenomenon literally.
In ordinary language, the phenomenon is effectively treated as “the thing itself.”
In philosophical language, by contrast, the phenomenon is precisely the appearance of the thing, not the thing apart from its manifestation.
Every phenomenon is certainly the phenomenon of something—a real natural thing, a human being, an ideal entity.
But it is also always the appearance of that thing, and therefore the appearance of that thing to someone.
As I have already said, what appears can be absolutely anything. Its phenomenon can therefore also be anything.
And it can appear to, so to speak, “anyone.”
But since by phenomenon we mean the appearance of something to a person, that “someone” can only be a human being.
A phenomenon, then, is anything that appears to a human being, regardless of what appears or, so to speak, to whom it appears.
